prs.body:
## High Level Overview of Change

fixAMMv1_1 has been enabled on mainnet long enough to retire, so move
its macro to the retired list and delete the conditional code it
guarded, keeping the enabled behavior.

Removed gates: changeSpotPriceQuality, swapAssetIn and swapAssetOut in
AMMHelpers.h; adjustAmountsByLPTokens in AMMHelpers.cpp; accountSendIOU
in TokenHelpers.cpp; the LP token balance checks in AMMWithdraw.cpp;
and adjustQualityWithFees plus the two qualityThreshold lambdas in
BookStep.cpp.

Three parameters became dead and are dropped with their call sites: the
Rules argument of changeSpotPriceQuality, and the Rules argument of
both adjustQualityWithFees overloads. BookStep.cpp no longer needs
Rules.h.

One behavior change is worth noting. swapAssetIn and swapAssetOut read
the amendment through getCurrentTransactionRules(), which is only
seated during transaction application. Path finding reaches them
through RippleCalc::rippleCalculate from Pathfinder and PathRequest,
where it is unseated, so ripple_path_find and path_find have been using
the pre-fix swap math while the transactors used the post-fix math.
Retiring the amendment makes both paths agree. This is RPC-visible but
not consensus-relevant, since path finding only proposes paths and the
Payment transactor executes them.

adjustAmountsByLPTokens is unaffected: its only callers are
AMMDeposit::deposit and AMMWithdraw::withdraw, both reached solely
through doApply, where Transactor::operator() seats the rules
unconditionally.

## API Impact

- [ ] Public API: New feature (new methods and/or new fields)
- [ ] Public API: Breaking change (in general, breaking changes should only impact the next api_version)
- [x] `libxrpl` change (any change that may affect `libxrpl` or dependents of `libxrpl`)
- [ ] Peer protocol change (must be backward compatible or bump the peer protocol version)

## Test Plan

Updated AMM_test.cpp, AMMExtended_test.cpp, AMMMPT_test.cpp, and AMMCalc_test.cpp

prs.body:
## High Level Overview of Change

Introduces `fixAMMOfferRounding` (subsequently combined with #5016 and renamed to `fixAMMv1_1`) amendment to improve quality of the generated AMM offer for a single path payment when one side of the offer is XRP and there is a Limit Order Book (LOB) offer for the same asset pair on the DEX.

### Context of Change

A single-path AMM offer with account offer on DEX, is always generated
starting with the takerPays first, which is rounded up, and then
the takerGets, which is rounded down. This rounding ensures that the pool's
product invariant is maintained. However, when one of the offer's side
is XRP, this rounding can result in the AMM offer having a lower
quality, potentially causing offer generation to fail if the quality
is lower than the account's offer quality.
    
To address this issue, the proposed fix adjusts the offer generation process
to start with the XRP side first and always rounds it down. This results
in a smaller offer size, improving the offer's quality.
This change still ensures the product invariant, as the other generated
side is the exact result of the swap-in or swap-out equations.

### API Impact

reviewCommentsList.author: HowardHinnant
reviewCommentsList.body:
These are clever.  And I like the way they clean up the code.  But @scottschurr pointed out to me a potential to cause a run-time error:  Subexpressions in C++ are not guaranteed to be executed in any given order.  See: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/eval_order#:~:text=Order%20of%20evaluation%20of%20any,same%20expression%20is%20evaluated%20again.

For example in:
```c++
z = downward()(a * b) / upward()(c - d);
```
I am concerned that the order could be:
1. construct downward
2. construct upward
3. execute a * b
4. execute c - d
5. call the downward() with a*b
6. call the upward with c-d
7. do the division

When I tried to simulate such an order with clang, I failed to do so.  But even if all of our compilers don't create a run-time error now, if they started to in the future, the error would be silent, and extremely subtle, hard to detect and hard to find and fix.

reviewCommentsList.author: scottschurr

Well, if you can find a place in the standard that says parenthesis will guarantee that order, please add that reference to the source code in a comment.  I don't know the standard well enough to have a sense for where you might find such a guarantee.  However there are several places in the standard that say, to a large extent, order of evaluation within an expression is unspecified.

The standard has specific rules about constructors and destructors.  That's why RAII works.  But here we have a constructor and the function call operator.  It's not the same thing.

reviewCommentsList.body: There are two scenario. One is - AMM offer is generated so that the new Spot Price Quality is equal to the requested quality. In this case the offer's quality is better than updated SPQ. The second is - if there is a trading fee then matching the new SPQ to the target quality will push AMM offer quality bellow the target quality. In this case the AMM offer is generated to match the target quality and SPQ quality is going to be better than the target quality. In both cases we start the offer generation with the XRP side (if applicable) and we round it downward. This minimizes the offer size and maximizes the quality. If the offer is IOU/IOU, we still round downward the side of the offer that we start generating first. This again minimizes the offer and maximizes the quality. So the scenario when we succeed in the offer generation but it's quality is less than the target quality should be pretty rare. It's still possible though and perhaps we should add some error allowance.

Just a general comment, not necessarily related to this bit of code:  I'm beginning to question the wisdom of directed rounding on every single operation.  The one other place I've seen this done is when one is trying to put lower and upper limits on the exact answer.  One does the computation twice, with consistent rounding one way, and then the other.

That's not what we're trying to do here.  What we want is to compute as accurately as possible, but make sure that round off error doesn't violate an invariant, such as creating XRP.  Perhaps we should stick to round_to_nearest, but then clip the final result to meet our invariants.  Perhaps clipping the final result, as opposed to rounding individual operations is the better tool here.
